title: 4 Residency Block Schedule Tools (One Done For You)
description: Residency block schedule software compared: QGenda, Amion, the spreadsheet and a done-for-you service, by who builds it and where the ACGME rules go in.
content:
Summary

  • Choosing residency scheduling software comes down to one key decision: do you want to operate the tool yourself (DIY) or have the schedule built for you (managed service)?
  • Self-service tools need someone to learn them and configure the ACGME rules, which is hard to sustain when the chief changes every year.
  • This guide compares four options, breaking down their operating models, ACGME compliance features, and learning curves to help you find the right fit.
  • For programs looking to get dozens of hours back, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard delivers finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, with no software to learn.

If you've ever sat down to build a residency block schedule, you already know the feeling. It's "a painful and tedious process", as one chief resident put it, involving fragile spreadsheets, dozens of exceptions, and a sinking sense that one wrong cell formula could blow up three months of planning. Another resident summed it up: even Excel with a couple of self-written scripts is still the most annoying part of the job.

There are options beyond Excel, but they work in different ways, and the right choice depends on which camp you fall into.

Camp 1, the DIY operator: You want to run the software yourself. You're willing to invest a few days (or weeks) upfront to learn a tool, configure rules, and manage the schedule on an ongoing basis. You want control.

Camp 2, the delegation seeker: You want someone else to build the schedule for you. You don't have the bandwidth to learn new software, you're inheriting scheduling responsibilities mid-cycle, or you're tired of institutional knowledge walking out the door every time a new chief rotates in.

This guide covers four options, a done-for-you managed service, the spreadsheet, an enterprise platform and a publishing platform, with a breakdown of ACGME compliance, learning curve, specialty support, and pricing.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

1. Scheduling Wizard, The Done-For-You Managed Service

Best For: Chief residents, program directors, and GME coordinators who want to hand the scheduling burden off and receive the finished schedule, built to the requirements they tell us apply.

Scheduling Wizard is the one on this list that isn't software in the traditional sense. It's a managed scheduling service, meaning you don't log into a platform and build anything. Instead, you submit your rules (rotation requirements, vacation requests, program-specific rules, subspecialty coverage needs), and our team produces the block, clinic, call and attending schedules, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

It is a different model from the rest of the list, aimed at a different problem.

Key Features:

  • No software to learn. Nothing to configure, no rule-writer, no training.
  • Built around GME rules from the start.
  • The ACGME requirements you tell us apply are built in, not checked after the fact. The subspecialty requirements you tell us apply are built in too.
  • Institutional continuity across chief rotations: scheduling knowledge doesn't walk out the door every July.
  • Handles multi-schedule dependencies: Block, Call, Clinic, and Attending schedules are built in coordination, not in isolation.
  • Resident preferences (vacation, electives, conferences, moonlighting) are part of the build.
  • Your platform, your choice: upload the finished files into the platform you already run, use our live view, or both.

ACGME Compliance: Core to the service. The requirements you tell us apply are built into the schedule, not left to you to configure.

Learning Curve: None. That's the point.

Pricing: quoted per program.

Pros:

  • Takes dozens of hours of chief resident work off the program
  • The ACGME requirements you give us are built in while the schedule is made
  • Keeps the rules written down through chief turnover
  • Leaves the platform choice to you (Amion, QGenda, our live view, or both)

Cons:

  • Not the right fit if your program wants hands-on, day-to-day schedule control
  • No self-service platform for real-time edits; revisions are handled by our team

What you get: the finished block schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, and a custom live view of it if that is useful to your program. Redrafts are included, not billed separately, which matters most on a block schedule because one change in February moves the rest of the year. For the specifics, see our page on residency block schedules. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel / Google Sheets, The Actual Incumbent

Best For: Programs with unusual rotation structures, multi-track years, or requirements that are hard to express in a block builder.

Many residency block schedules started life as a spreadsheet, and many still are one. It sits second because nothing beats it for expressiveness. A year-long grid with PGY-level tracks, split rotations, away electives and three residents on modified schedules is something you can simply lay out in cells.

Block schedules are also where the arithmetic gets heavy. Rotation minimums, vacation coverage and the knock-on effects into call and clinic all have to hold at once, across a year. A spreadsheet will show you the grid without telling you which requirement you just broke, and the logic behind it leaves with whoever built it.

3. QGenda: The Enterprise-Grade Self-Service Platform

Best For: Large health systems needing a single, scalable scheduling platform across multiple departments and provider types.

QGenda is an enterprise scheduling platform for healthcare. Its combination of a rule writer and autoscheduling features means that, if set up properly, it does a lot of the heavy lifting.

Key Features:

  • Enterprise-grade rule configuration that can model highly complex scheduling rules
  • Real-time visibility, automated shift alerts, and reporting dashboards
  • Integrations with EHRs including Epic and Cerner
  • Mobile access for residents and attendings

ACGME Compliance: QGenda can hold ACGME rules once your team configures them in the rule writer.

Learning Curve: Front-loaded. As one Reddit user noted: "QGenda is a TON of work upfront but then is basically set and forget after that." The problem is that "a ton of work upfront" is exactly what a one-year chief resident doesn't have.

Pricing: Quoted by the vendor; ask them directly.

Pros: Scalable and highly configurable for complex health systems
Cons: Setup takes real time up front, and someone has to own the rules when the chief changes

4. Amion: The Familiar Publishing Platform

Best For: Programs that need a simple tool to publish schedules and manage basic shift swaps.

Amion is a well-known name in residency scheduling, but its reputation is as a publishing platform, not a builder. Many programs that use Amion create the schedule in Excel, then upload it to Amion for residents to view and swap shifts.

Key Features:

  • Online schedule publishing and viewing
  • Resident-initiated shift swapping
  • Email/pager on-call notifications

ACGME Compliance: Sits with whoever builds the schedule before it is published.

Learning Curve: Low for basic viewing. The schedule creation problem, the painful, tedious part, still lives in your spreadsheet. As one resident put it: "We used Amion. Being able to swap between ourselves was fine." Fine for swapping; doesn't solve building.

Pricing: Ask the vendor.

Pros: Familiar to most residents; good for publishing and swaps
Cons: The schedule, and the ACGME checks, are built elsewhere

How to Choose a Residency Block Schedule Tool

The bigger decision is less about features than about how your program operates. Do you want to build and manage a schedule, or do you want to receive one?

A simple decision matrix:

Your Situation Best Fit
Large health system, need enterprise scalability QGenda
Need a simple way to publish the schedule plus shift swapping Amion
No time to learn software, need ACGME rules built in from the start, tired of losing institutional knowledge every July Scheduling Wizard

The right self-service tool for your program depends on your tech comfort level, institutional size, and how much chief resident bandwidth you're willing to invest. A study of one residency's rebuilt call schedule found call variation fell by 70% and perceived fairness rose from 43% to 95%. Self-service tools can get part of the way there, but only if someone configures and runs them correctly, every year.

That is the hard part in residency settings specifically: the person doing the configuring changes every year, the institutional knowledge resets, and the compliance burden lives entirely with a chief resident who's also, you know, practicing medicine.

If that sounds like your program, a managed service may fit better than another piece of software.

Scheduling Wizard is the only dedicated managed service on this list. You submit your rules. The team delivers the finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules, built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for whatever viewing platform you already use. There is no ramp-up or rule-writing on your side, and the rules stay written down when the chief changes.

If you would rather review a finished block schedule than build one, talk to us.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you handle ACGME rules across different subspecialties?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Does Scheduling Wizard replace our Amion account?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What is the process of getting a schedule built by a managed service?

The process involves three main steps: submitting your program's specific rules, receiving a draft schedule for review, and getting a final, ready-to-use schedule. First, you'll provide all your requirements through a structured intake process, this includes rotation rules, individual vacation requests, clinic assignments, and any unique program needs. Our team then builds the schedule. You review the draft, request any tweaks, and we deliver the final version as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for distribution or upload to your viewing platform.

What happens if we need to make changes to the schedule mid-year?

Mid-year changes, such as unexpected resident leave or rotation adjustments, are handled directly by the Scheduling Wizard team. While you don't have a self-service platform for real-time edits, our service model includes support for revisions. You contact our team with the change, and we rebuild to the same rules and deliver an updated schedule. Redrafts are part of the service.

When should a program choose a managed service over a DIY scheduling tool?

You should choose a managed service if your primary goal is to save time, keep schedules inside the ACGME rules without manual effort, and maintain scheduling continuity despite annual chief resident turnover. DIY tools are a good fit for programs that have dedicated administrative time and want hands-on control. However, if your chief residents are overwhelmed, if you're concerned about rules being configured incorrectly, or if you lose valuable scheduling knowledge every July, a managed service is likely the better fit.

What types of schedules can Scheduling Wizard create?

Scheduling Wizard can create complex, interdependent schedules for your entire program, including Block, Call, Clinic, and Attending schedules. A key advantage is that we build these schedules together. For example, we know that a resident's block assignment impacts their availability for call and clinic duties. Building them together avoids many of the conflicts and coverage gaps that come from building them separately.
